sections.html:
Amherst is a college town of about 39,263 people (2020 census) in Hampshire County, in the Connecticut River valley roughly 22 miles north of Springfield. The census estimate for 2025 is 40,920. There are 9,711 housing units, and the town includes three communities: Amherst Center, North Amherst and South Amherst. ZIP codes are 01002, 01003 (UMass) and 01059 (North Amherst).

The University of Massachusetts Amherst, Amherst College and Hampshire College shape the market. Housing leans toward rentals and small households, so a seller usually meets two kinds of buyer: owner-occupants who want to be near the schools and campuses, and investors who count on tenants. If your house is already a rental, it has to meet the town's rental rules.

Amherst requires registration of residential rental property, and permits must be renewed every year by June 15. Inspections are now a condition of keeping a permit.

Rental ruleWhat Amherst requires
RegistrationEvery residential rental, renewed each year by June 15
Inspection programUp to 500 randomly selected units a year, out of more than 5,000 rentals
RecyclingEvery permit must include a recycling plan
How to applyOnline through the town's portal

The Inspection Services Department runs the Residential Rental Property Inspection Program, which is expected to continue for several years. Owners receive a postcard when their unit is picked. The rental bylaw was adopted on April 8, 2024.

If you own a rental and plan to sell, call Inspection Services at 413-259-3030 or inspections@amherstma.gov. Ask about your permit status and any open inspection before you agree to a closing date.

Amherst has a town council and a town manager. Massachusetts treats it as a city, but it keeps "Town of" in its name. Voters approved the charter in March 2018 with 58 percent, and a 13-member council took office on December 2, 2018. Ten councilors represent districts, two per district, and three serve at large. The council appoints the manager.

Local rules such as the rental bylaw above are adopted through this council.

Winters are cold and snowy, and summers are warm. Buyers and inspectors pay close attention to heating, roofs and insulation. A seller with an aging furnace, an older roof or an uninsulated attic should expect the buyer to raise it, and should decide ahead of time whether to repair, credit the buyer or sell as-is.

Massachusetts rules decide most of the timeline here. The Appellate Tax Board's appeals guide spells them out.

  • A town that bills quarterly generally collects on August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1.
  • An abatement application must be in by the first installment date of the actual bill, generally February 1 in quarterly towns.
  • The assessors get three months to respond. An appeal to the board must follow within three months of what they do.

Call the Amherst Assessors for the current rate and the exact bill dates. Letting a bill go unpaid starts the process in the Land Court's foreclosure overview: a demand after 30 days, a possible tax taking 14 days later, and a right to redeem until a court judgment.

A one or two family home needs a smoke and carbon monoxide compliance certificate before it can transfer. A rental needs its permit in good order.

The state's alarm inspection guide says to call the local fire department once you have a closing date. The department charges a fee for the inspection and certificate. An alarm with no manufacture date counts as expired.

Whoever the buyer is, the certificate is part of the transfer. Agree in writing which side books the inspection and pays the fee, so no one is surprised at closing.

A rental house sale has a few extra moving parts.

  1. Confirm the permit is current and note the June 15 renewal date.
  2. Ask Inspection Services whether your unit has been picked for inspection or has an open item.
  3. Check whether any tenant is still in place and what notice the lease requires.
  4. Book the alarm inspection when a closing date is set.
  5. Have your closing attorney confirm the tax payoff.

Cash Home Buyers purchases Amherst houses as-is, including worn-out rentals and inherited homes, so you can skip repairs and showings. Reach out for an offer, and compare it with what a listing would net after repairs and weeks on the market.

The tradeoff is time and effort against price.

A listing exposes the house to many buyers, which helps a well-kept home near campus. It can also bring weeks of showings and repair requests. A direct cash purchase suits an owner with a tired rental, an inherited house or a deadline, because there are no showings and the buyer takes the house as is. Expect the price to reflect the repairs the buyer takes on.

faqs.q: How many people live in Amherst, Massachusetts?
faqs.a: The 2020 census counted 39,263 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 40,920. Many are students at the three local colleges.

faqs.q: Do I need a rental permit in Amherst?
faqs.a: Yes. Amherst requires registration of residential rental property, renewed each year by June 15, and rental units are subject to inspection.

faqs.q: How often will Amherst inspect a rental property?
faqs.a: Up to 500 randomly selected units are inspected each year across more than 5,000 rentals, so some owners may wait years to be picked.

faqs.q: Is Amherst a town or a city?
faqs.a: Both in a legal sense. Massachusetts treats it as a city because of its council-manager charter, but it keeps the name Town of Amherst.

faqs.q: Do I need a smoke detector certificate to sell in Amherst?
faqs.a: For a one or two family home, yes. The local fire department inspects and issues a certificate of compliance, and it charges a fee.
